worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: Is f(x)=x^2+3 continuous at x=−2? State the value and the relevant limit.
steps: Polynomials are continuous at every real input.
Direct substitution gives f(−2)=4+3=7, matching the limit.

items.prompt: For x≠0 let g(x)=sin x/x, and let g(0)=4. Using the standard sine limit 1, test continuity at zero.
items.answer: Not continuous; the limit is 1 but g(0)=4.
steps: The supplied limit exists.
Its disagreement with the assigned value violates the third continuity condition.

items.prompt: Where is r(x)=1/(x^2−16) discontinuous?
steps: The denominator vanishes exactly at those two inputs.
Rational functions are continuous at every other input in their domain.

items.prompt: Choose c to make f(x)=x+2 for x<3 and f(x)=c for x≥3 continuous at 3.
steps: The left limit is 3+2=5.
The right limit and actual value are both c, so all three must equal 5.

items.prompt: Can a new value at x=0 make f(x)=−1 for x<0 and f(x)=1 for x>0 continuous there?
steps: The one-sided limits are −1 and 1.
A single assigned value cannot make unequal sides share a common limit.

items.prompt: Is √x continuous at the left endpoint x=0 of its domain?
steps: The function is defined at zero with value zero.
Inputs within its domain approach from the right, and their roots approach that same value.

worksheets.title: Use existence hypotheses
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: Find k so f(x)=(x^2−9)/(x−3) for x≠3 and f(3)=k is continuous everywhere.
steps: The only removed input is 3, and the nearby formula simplifies to x+3.
Assigning its limiting value 6 repairs that sole hole.

items.prompt: For f(x)=ax+1 when x≤2 and f(x)=x^2−1 when x>2, find a for continuity at 2.
steps: The right limit is 4−1=3.
The left limit and value are 2a+1, so set 2a+1=3.

items.prompt: Explain why endpoint signs of f(x)=1/x on [−1,1] do not guarantee a zero.
items.answer: The function is not continuous or even defined at zero.
steps: Its endpoint values have opposite signs.
The missing continuity hypothesis blocks the theorem, and 1/x never equals zero.

items.prompt: For continuous f on [2,5] with f(2)=7 and f(5)=−1, is f(c)=3 guaranteed for some c in (2,5)?
steps: The target 3 lies strictly between −1 and 7.
Continuity on the full closed interval allows the Intermediate Value Theorem.

items.prompt: For continuous g on [0,4] with g(0)=2 and g(4)=6, is g(c)=8 guaranteed?
steps: Eight is outside the interval of endpoint values.
The line g(x)=x+2 meets all givens but never reaches 8 on [0,4].

items.prompt: Show that x^2−2 has a zero between 1 and 2, then narrow the guarantee to (1,1.5).
steps: The continuous polynomial has values −1 at 1 and 2 at 2.
Its value at 1.5 is 0.25, still opposite in sign to the value at 1, so the smaller interval works.

worksheets.title: Build and critique continuous models
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: A continuous temperature record is 12°C at 8 a.m. and 19°C at noon. What can be concluded about reaching 16°C, and can its exact time be inferred?
items.answer: It reaches 16°C at least once between 8 a.m. and noon; the exact time is undetermined.
steps: Sixteen is between the two endpoint temperatures.
Continuity guarantees a time but does not specify the shape or speed of the warming.

items.prompt: A device reports floor(t), the greatest integer ≤t. Is its output continuous at t=2?
items.answer: No; the left limit is 1 while the value and right limit are 2.
steps: Just below 2, the greatest integer not exceeding t is 1.
At and just above 2 the value is 2, producing a jump.

items.prompt: Does continuity with opposite endpoint signs guarantee exactly one zero? Give a polynomial counterexample on [−2,2].
items.answer: No; f(x)=x(x^2−1) has zeros −1,0,1 and opposite endpoint signs.
steps: Its values at −2 and 2 are −6 and 6.
It is continuous yet has three zeros, disproving uniqueness.

items.prompt: Construct a continuous piecewise rule using x^2 for x≤1 and a linear rule of slope 3 for x>1.
steps: The left value at 1 is 1.
A line 3x+b must satisfy 3+b=1, so b=−2 joins the branches.

items.prompt: For f(x)=√(x−1)/(x−4), state every interval of continuity within the real domain.
steps: The root requires x≥1 and the denominator excludes 4.
Continuous component functions combine continuously at every remaining input.

items.prompt: A student says a continuous curve with f(0)=f(2)=3 must be constant. Give a counterexample and verify the endpoints.
steps: Substituting 0 or 2 makes the added product zero, giving 3.
At x=1 the value is 4, so a continuous curve can leave and return to the same height.

weeks.title: Derivatives from a limiting quotient
weeks.objective: Compute and interpret a derivative from its definition, including one-sided failure.

connection.before: Limits describe the trend of secant slopes as the increment approaches zero.
connection.after: Power and sum rules will shorten computations already grounded in this definition.

days: Build the derivative quotient at a point.
Simplify with h≠0 before taking a limit.
Derive a derivative function for a quadratic.
Compare corner slopes and smooth slopes.
Translate a derivative between symbols, graph, and units.
explanation: The derivative f′(a) is the limit as h→0 of (f(a+h)−f(a))/h, when that limit is a finite real number. Each nonzero h gives a secant slope; the limit gives the tangent slope at the base point. The symbol f′(a) denotes a number, whereas f′(x) denotes a new function assigning a slope to every input where the derivative exists.

Use the definition in three stages: substitute the entire input a+h, simplify while h≠0, then take the limit. A common factor h may cancel even though h=0 was excluded in the original quotient, because a limit concerns nearby inputs. The derivative of a quadratic can therefore be found exactly from an expression whose original direct substitution would have been 0/0.

A finite derivative requires matching limiting slopes from both sides. At a corner, the function can be continuous while its one-sided slopes disagree. At a vertical tangent, slopes may grow without bound rather than approach a finite derivative. Differentiability implies continuity, but continuity alone does not guarantee differentiability; inspecting heights and inspecting slopes answer different questions.

examples.prompt: Use the definition to find f′(2) for f(x)=x^2+1.
steps: The quotient is [(2+h)^2+1−5]/h for h≠0.
Expansion and cancellation give (4h+h^2)/h=4+h.
Taking h→0 gives 4, the tangent slope at the point (2,5).

examples.prompt: Use the definition to find the derivative function of f(x)=1/x.
steps: The quotient is [1/(x+h)−1/x]/h, with both inputs nonzero.
A common denominator reduces it to −1/[x(x+h)].
Taking h→0 gives −1/x^2 wherever the original function is defined.

worksheets.title: Read and compute derivative definitions
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: Use the derivative definition to find f′(1) for f(x)=x^2+2x.
steps: Expanding f(1+h)−f(1) gives 4h+h^2.
Dividing by h and taking its limit gives 4.

items.prompt: For g(x)=7x−3, write its difference quotient and derivative.
steps: The output change is 7h.
For h≠0 the quotient is already 7, so its limit is 7.

items.prompt: Find the derivative of the constant function f(x)=−5 from the definition.
steps: Both function values in the numerator equal −5.
Every nonzero-increment quotient is zero, so the limit is zero.

items.prompt: The quotient for p at a is 6+2h for h≠0. Find p′(a).
steps: The derivative is the limit of the given quotient.
The term 2h tends to zero, leaving 6.

items.prompt: Which derivative is represented by lim as h→0 of [(3+h)^3−27]/h?
steps: The base output is f(3)=27.
The other output is f(3+h), matching the derivative definition at 3.

items.prompt: For f(x)=x^2, find the equation of the tangent at x=−1 using f′(−1)=−2.
steps: The point on the curve is (−1,1).
Insert slope −2 into y−1=−2(x+1) and simplify.

worksheets.title: Derive and compare slope functions
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: Derive f′(x) from the definition for f(x)=3x^2.
steps: The output change expands to 6xh+3h^2.
After division by h, the limit of 6x+3h is 6x.

items.prompt: At a>0, rationalize the definition quotient for f(x)=√x to find f′(a).
steps: The quotient reduces to 1/(√(a+h)+√a) by multiplying by the conjugate.
Its denominator tends to 2√a, which is nonzero for a>0.

items.prompt: For f(x)=abs(x−2), compare one-sided derivative quotients at 2.
items.answer: Left −1, right 1; f′(2) does not exist.
steps: Since f(2)=0, the quotient is abs(h)/h.
Its value is −1 for negative h and 1 for positive h, preventing a common limit.

items.prompt: Evaluate lim as x→4 of (x^2−16)/(x−4), and identify the derivative it represents.
steps: The quotient compares f(x) with f(4) over the matching input difference.
Factoring gives x+4, whose limit is 8.

items.prompt: Let f(x)=x^2 for x<0 and f(x)=2x^2 for x≥0. Is it differentiable at zero?
steps: Its difference quotient is h for h<0 and 2h for h>0.
Both tend to zero, and f(0)=0 matches both branch heights.

items.prompt: A student replaces f(x+h) by f(x)+f(h) for f(x)=x^2. Show the missing term.
steps: The actual expansion is x^2+2xh+h^2.
The proposed sum x^2+h^2 omits the cross term, changing the derivative.

worksheets.title: Interpret differentiability
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: A volume V(t) in liters has V′(5)=−2. State the meaning, including units.
items.answer: At t=5 the volume is decreasing instantaneously at 2 liters per unit of t.
steps: A derivative measures output change per input change at the specified input.
The negative sign means decreasing volume; the time unit must be whatever unit t uses.

items.prompt: For f(x)=x^(1/3), what happens to [f(h)−f(0)]/h as h→0 through nonzero real h? Is there a finite derivative?
items.answer: It grows to +∞; no finite derivative exists at zero.
steps: The quotient equals 1/(h^(2/3)), positive on both sides.
Its denominator tends to zero, creating a vertical tangent rather than a finite slope.

items.prompt: Suppose f′(a)=3. Does this force f(a)=3? Give a linear counterexample.
items.answer: No; f(x)=3x+10 at a=0 has derivative 3 and value 10.
steps: The derivative describes slope rather than height.
Adding a constant changes height without changing the derivative.

items.prompt: For s(t)=t^2−4t meters, derive the instantaneous velocity at t=3 seconds.
steps: The quotient [s(3+h)−s(3)]/h simplifies to 2+h.
Its limit is 2, with position-per-time units.

items.prompt: Construct a differentiable function with value 4 and derivative −3 at x=2.
steps: Substituting x=2 gives the required height 4.
Its constant difference quotient is −3, giving the required derivative.

items.prompt: Why is directly setting h=0 in the original derivative quotient invalid even for a smooth polynomial?
items.answer: It creates division by zero; the derivative is a limit of quotients at nonzero h.
steps: The numerator also becomes zero, producing 0/0 rather than a number.
Simplification on nearby inputs followed by a limit determines the derivative.

weeks.title: Power rules and tangent lines
weeks.objective: Differentiate power sums and use a slope with a curve point to construct a tangent.

connection.before: The derivative definition produces exact slopes but can require long expansions.
connection.after: First and second derivatives will describe velocity, acceleration, and smoothness.

days: Connect the power rule to definition-based examples.
Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers.
Apply sum and constant-multiple rules.
Build tangent equations with both slope and height.
Solve a derivative condition and check the original curve.
explanation: For a power x^n, the derivative is n x^(n−1) on an interval where the original power and derivative are defined. A constant differentiates to zero; a constant multiplier remains outside the derivative; and a sum differentiates term by term. These are proven consequences of the derivative definition, not new definitions. Reducing the exponent without multiplying by the old exponent misses part of the rule.

Rewrite reciprocal and root expressions with exponents before applying a power rule. For example, 1/x^3 is x^(−3), so its derivative has both a negative coefficient and a more negative exponent. Fractional powers require domain care. A square root is defined at zero, but its derivative formula has zero in the denominator there and supplies no finite derivative at that endpoint.

A tangent line needs a point and a slope. First evaluate y0=f(a), then find m=f′(a), and use y−y0=m(x−a). The derivative alone is not the line equation, because it does not specify the line’s height. A horizontal tangent requires f′(a)=0 at a point where the function and derivative exist; solving that equation can yield several inputs.

examples.prompt: Differentiate f(x)=2x^4−3x^2+5x−8 and find f′(1).
steps: Apply the power rule to each nonconstant term.
The constant −8 contributes zero, so the derivative is 8x^3−6x+5.
Substituting 1 gives 8−6+5=7.

examples.prompt: Find the tangent to f(x)=√x at x=9.
steps: The point is (9,3).
Rewriting as x^(1/2) gives f′(x)=1/(2√x), so the slope is 1/6.
Use point-slope form with that point and slope.

worksheets.title: Apply power and sum rules
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: Differentiate f(x)=x^5−4x+2.
steps: The fifth power contributes 5x^4 and the linear term contributes −4.
The constant 2 contributes zero.

items.prompt: Find d/dx of 6/x^2 for x≠0.
steps: Write the expression as 6x^(−2).
Multiply by −2 and reduce the exponent to −3.

items.prompt: Differentiate 4√x for x>0.
steps: Rewrite as 4x^(1/2).
The coefficient becomes 4(1/2)=2 and the new exponent is −1/2.
The derivative is 9x^2−4x.
At −1 this gives 9+4=13.

items.prompt: Find the tangent slope of y=5−2x^2 at x=3.
steps: The derivative of the constant is zero and of −2x^2 is −4x.
Evaluating at 3 gives −12.

items.prompt: Find all horizontal-tangent inputs for f(x)=x^2−8x+1.
steps: Differentiate to obtain 2x−8.
Set it equal to zero and solve; the polynomial is defined there.

worksheets.title: Combine slope with position
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: Find the tangent line to f(x)=x^3−x at x=2.
steps: The curve value is 8−2=6.
The derivative 3x^2−1 gives slope 11 at 2.

items.prompt: Differentiate (x^3+2x)/x for x≠0 using simplification first.
steps: The original rule equals x^2+2 on nonzero inputs.
Differentiating gives 2x, but simplification does not make the original function defined at zero.

items.prompt: Find the derivative of x^(3/2)−x^(−1/2) for x>0.
steps: Apply the rule separately to both fractional powers.
The negative coefficient of the second term multiplies its negative exponent, giving a positive contribution.

items.prompt: For f(x)=ax^2+2x, find a if f′(3)=14.
steps: Differentiate to get f′(x)=2ax+2.
The condition gives 6a+2=14, hence a=2.

items.prompt: A student gives the tangent y=6x for f(x)=x^2+5 at x=3. Correct the line.
steps: The slope 6 is correct.
The line must pass through (3,14), which y=6x does not.

items.prompt: Find all points where f(x)=x^3−3x has a horizontal tangent.
steps: Solve f′(x)=3x^2−3=0 to get x=±1.
Substitute each input into the original function to obtain the point heights.

worksheets.title: Use derivative conditions
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: A cost C(q)=0.5q^2+7q+40 dollars is modeled continuously. Find marginal cost at q=10 and interpret it as a local rate.
steps: Differentiation gives C′(q)=q+7.
At q=10 the instantaneous modeled increase is 17 dollars per added unit; a whole-unit cost change is only approximated by this rate.

items.prompt: Find a quadratic f(x)=ax^2+b with f(2)=9 and f′(2)=8.
steps: The derivative condition gives 4a=8, so a=2.
The value condition becomes 8+b=9, giving b=1.

items.prompt: For f(x)=1/x, find the tangent line at x=−2.
steps: The point has height −1/2.
The derivative −1/x^2 has value −1/4 at −2, fixing the point-slope equation.

items.prompt: Can a polynomial with derivative 4x^3−2 have the form x^4−2x+C? Explain the role of C.
items.answer: Yes; any real constant C works.
steps: Differentiating x^4−2x gives 4x^3−2.
A constant contributes zero, so the derivative alone cannot determine vertical position.

items.prompt: For f(x)=x^4−2x^2, find every input where the tangent has slope zero and list the function values.
steps: Factor f′(x)=4x(x^2−1), giving the three inputs.
Substitute them into x^4−2x^2 rather than into the derivative to find heights.

items.prompt: Compare f(x)=x^2 and g(x)=x^2+100: where do they have equal derivative values, and do their tangent lines at the same input coincide?
items.answer: Derivatives agree everywhere; the tangent lines are parallel but distinct.
steps: Both derivatives are 2x.
Their tangent points differ vertically by 100, so equal slopes do not make the lines identical.

weeks.title: Motion, derivative units, and smoothness
weeks.objective: Relate position, velocity, acceleration, and speed while recognizing failures of differentiability.

connection.before: Differentiate power sums and interpret tangent slopes.
connection.after: Products, quotients, and compositions will expand the functions whose rates can be found.

days: Differentiate position to velocity and acceleration.
Distinguish direction from speeding up.
Translate derivative units in several contexts.
Check corners, jumps, and vertical tangents.
Analyze a complete time interval with turning points.
explanation: If s(t) is position along a line, velocity is v(t)=s′(t) and acceleration is a(t)=v′(t). Position in meters and time in seconds produce velocity in m/s and acceleration in m/s^2. Velocity carries direction; speed is abs(v). Positive acceleration means velocity is increasing, not automatically that speed is increasing. Away from v=0, speed increases when velocity and acceleration have the same sign.

A particle changes direction when velocity changes sign. An instant with v=0 is a candidate, but it may simply be a momentary stop without reversal. Test the signs on the time intervals around it. Also distinguish average velocity over an interval from instantaneous velocity at an instant; the first uses endpoint positions and the second uses a derivative.

Differentiability can fail at a jump, corner, cusp, or vertical tangent. A discontinuity automatically prevents a derivative. A continuous graph still needs finite, agreeing one-sided derivative limits. Piecewise formulas should therefore be checked first for equal heights, then for equal slopes. These tests prevent using a derivative formula from one branch at a boundary where no derivative exists.

examples.prompt: A particle has s(t)=t^3−6t^2+9t meters for 0≤t≤4 seconds. Find v, a, and whether it speeds up at t=2.
examples.answer: v(t)=3t^2−12t+9; a(t)=6t−12; at t=2 the instantaneous rate of change of speed is zero, and speed has a local maximum.
steps: Differentiate position once for v and again for a.
At t=2, v=−3 m/s and a=0 m/s^2.

Since v(2)≠0, the speed derivative is sign(v(2))a(2)=0. On (1,2) velocity and acceleration are both negative, so speed increases; on (2,3) their signs oppose, so speed decreases, giving a local speed maximum.

examples.prompt: Let f(x)=x^2 for x≤1 and f(x)=2x−1 for x>1. Test differentiability at 1.
examples.answer: It is differentiable there, with derivative 2.
steps: The left value and right limiting height are both 1, so the join is continuous.
The left slope approaches 2x=2.
The right branch has slope 2, so the one-sided derivatives match.

worksheets.title: Separate velocity and speed
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: For s(t)=4t^2−t+3 meters with t in seconds, find velocity and acceleration.
steps: Differentiate position term by term.
Differentiate velocity once more, keeping the extra time factor in the units.

items.prompt: If v(t)=t^2−4, find velocity and speed at t=1.
steps: Substitute 1 into the signed velocity formula.
Speed is the nonnegative magnitude of that result.

items.prompt: A particle has velocity −5 m/s and acceleration −2 m/s^2. Is it speeding up or slowing down?
steps: Negative acceleration makes its already negative velocity more negative.
The magnitude of velocity therefore grows because the signs agree.

items.prompt: A particle has velocity −4 m/s and acceleration 3 m/s^2. Is it speeding up or slowing down?
steps: Positive acceleration moves the negative velocity toward zero.
Opposite signs imply decreasing speed while the velocity remains negative.

items.prompt: If A(r) measures square centimeters and r centimeters, state the units of A′(r).
items.answer: Square centimeters per centimeter, equivalently centimeters.
steps: A derivative divides output units by input units.
Simplifying cm^2/cm gives cm, though the rate interpretation remains area change per radius change.

items.prompt: For v(t)=(t−2)^2, does the particle reverse direction at t=2?
steps: Velocity is positive on both sides and zero only at 2.
A direction reversal requires a sign change, not merely a zero.

worksheets.title: Inspect derivative meaning and existence
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: For s(t)=t^3−3t meters on 0≤t≤2 seconds, identify when motion is to the left and right.
items.answer: Left on [0,1); right on (1,2]; stopped at 1.
steps: Velocity is 3t^2−3=3(t−1)(t+1).
On the given nonnegative interval its sign is negative before 1 and positive afterward.

items.prompt: For s(t)=2t^3−9t^2, find acceleration at t=2.
items.answer: 6 units of position per time squared.
steps: Differentiate twice to get v=6t^2−18t and a=12t−18.
Substitution gives 24−18=6.

items.prompt: A continuous piecewise graph has slope −2 immediately left of x=3 and slope 4 immediately right. Does f′(3) exist?
steps: The two one-sided derivative limits are −2 and 4.
Continuity of heights does not repair the unequal tangent slopes.

items.prompt: For f(x)=x^2 when x<0 and f(x)=x+1 when x≥0, explain why f′(0) fails without computing slopes.
items.answer: The function is discontinuous at zero, so it cannot be differentiable there.
steps: The left limiting height is 0 while f(0)=1.
Differentiability would force continuity, contradicting those heights.

items.prompt: Given f(x)=x^3, find f′(0) and f″(0). Does their equality mean f is constant near zero?
items.answer: Both are zero; f is not constant near zero.
steps: Differentiation gives 3x^2 and 6x, both zero at the origin.
But f(0.1)=0.001 differs from f(0), so pointwise derivative values do not fix a neighborhood.

items.prompt: A temperature T(t) is in degrees Celsius with t in minutes. Interpret T″(4)=−0.5.
items.answer: At minute 4, the temperature-change rate is decreasing at 0.5°C per minute per minute.
steps: The first derivative is a rate in °C/min.
Its derivative describes how that rate changes, in °C/min^2, not the temperature itself.

worksheets.title: Coordinate motion and smoothness
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: For v(t)=6−2t on 0≤t≤5, identify intervals of speeding up and slowing down.
items.answer: Slowing down on (0,3); speeding up on (3,5).
steps: Acceleration is constantly −2 while velocity changes sign at 3.
Before 3 the signs oppose; afterward both are negative.

items.prompt: A runner’s positions are s(0)=5 m and s(4)=5 m, while s′(2)=−3 m/s. Is there a contradiction?
steps: Equal endpoints give average velocity zero over four seconds.
Instantaneous motion can be negative at one time and balanced by positive motion elsewhere.

items.prompt: Choose a and b so f(x)=x^2 for x≤2 and f(x)=ax+b for x>2 is differentiable at 2.
steps: Matching slopes requires a=2(2)=4.
Matching heights then requires 2a+b=4, yielding b=−4.

items.prompt: For s(t)=t^4−4t^2, calculate velocity and acceleration at t=1, then classify the speed change.
steps: The derivatives are 4t^3−8t and 12t^2−8.
At 1 their opposite signs mean the magnitude of velocity is decreasing.

items.prompt: Can acceleration vanish at an instant while velocity is nonzero? Supply a polynomial position model at t=0.
items.answer: For example s(t)=t+t^3 gives v(0)=1 and a(0)=0.
steps: Its velocity is 1+3t^2.
Its acceleration is 6t, so the requested values occur together at zero.

items.prompt: For f(x)=abs(x)^3, determine whether f′(0) exists using the difference quotient.
steps: The quotient abs(h)^3/h equals h^2 for h>0 and −h^2 for h<0.
Both sides tend to zero, so an absolute-value symbol alone does not imply a corner.

weeks.title: Products and quotients of changing functions
weeks.objective: Apply the product and quotient rules and choose simplification when it improves verification.

connection.before: Power rules differentiate separate sums, but multiplying functions creates additional change.
connection.after: The chain rule will address a function applied inside another function.

days: Derive a product-rate interpretation.
Differentiate products with both terms changing.
Keep quotient subtraction in order.
Simplify a rational rule and compare methods.
Use derivative data from a table without inventing formulas.
explanation: If u and v both depend on x, the derivative of uv is u′v+uv′. Each term accounts for one factor changing while the other supplies its current size. Multiplying u′v′ is not the product rule: it loses both first-order contributions. A rectangular area whose length and width both change gives a concrete interpretation of the two terms.

For a quotient u/v with v≠0, the derivative is (u′v−uv′)/v^2. Preserve the numerator order: derivative of the top times the bottom, minus the top times derivative of the bottom. Parentheses protect the subtraction when either factor has several terms. The denominator is squared; it is not the derivative of v, and original domain restrictions remain in force.

Sometimes expanding a polynomial product or dividing an expression first is simpler than using a rule mechanically. Two correct methods must agree on the original domain. Tables containing u, v, u′, and v′ at the same input can determine a product or quotient derivative without determining either whole function. Always verify that the denominator value is nonzero before applying the quotient rule.

examples.prompt: Differentiate f(x)=(x^2+1)(3x−2).
steps: The factor derivatives are 2x and 3.
The product rule gives 2x(3x−2)+3(x^2+1).
Expanding and combining terms gives 9x^2−4x+3.

examples.prompt: Find the derivative of g(x)=(x+1)/(x−2), x≠2.
steps: The top and bottom derivatives both equal 1.
The quotient numerator is (x−2)−(x+1)=−3.
Divide by the squared original denominator and retain x≠2.

worksheets.title: Use both change contributions
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: Differentiate (x^2−3)(x+4).
steps: Product rule gives 2x(x+4)+(x^2−3).
Combining terms gives the stated quadratic.

items.prompt: Find d/dx of x^2/(x+1), for x≠−1.
steps: The quotient numerator is 2x(x+1)−x^2.
Simplifying to x^2+2x and factoring gives the answer.

items.prompt: Differentiate x^3(2x^2−5) by expansion.
steps: Expand the original function to 2x^5−5x^3.
Differentiate the two powers separately.
Insert the table values into u′v+uv′.
The numerator is 2(3)−6(−1)=12.
The denominator is 3^2=9, giving 12/9=4/3.

items.prompt: Why is the derivative of x·x not 1·1? Compute the correct derivative.
steps: Each factor contributes one change term: 1·x+x·1.
Their sum is 2x, agreeing with the derivative of x^2.

worksheets.title: Coordinate algebra and derivative rules
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: Differentiate (x^2+2)/x on its original domain.
steps: Divide first to write x+2/x.
Differentiate the linear and reciprocal terms, retaining the excluded input.

items.prompt: Find the tangent slope of y=(2x−1)/(x+3) at x=1.
steps: Quotient differentiation gives [2(x+3)−(2x−1)]/(x+3)^2=7/(x+3)^2.
At 1 the denominator is 16.

items.prompt: For positive x, differentiate √x(x−2).
steps: Product rule gives (x−2)/(2√x)+√x.
Put both terms over 2√x and combine the numerators.

items.prompt: Find every input where the derivative of f(x)=x/(x^2+1) is zero.
steps: Its derivative is (1−x^2)/(x^2+1)^2.
The positive denominator never vanishes, so only numerator zeros qualify.

items.prompt: Correct the proposed derivative of (x−4)/(x+4): [(x−4)−(x+4)]/(x+4)^2.
steps: The proposal reversed the quotient-rule numerator.
Correct order gives (x+4)−(x−4)=8.

items.prompt: At x=0, f=2, f′=3, g=−1, g′=5. Find the derivative of 2fg−g^2 there.
steps: Differentiate to 2(f′g+fg′)−2gg′.
Insert the values: 2(−3+10)−2(−1)(5)=24.

worksheets.title: Model product and ratio rates
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: A rectangle has length L(t)=t+3 cm and width W(t)=2t+1 cm, with t in seconds. Find its area growth rate at t=2.
steps: At 2 the dimensions are 5 and 5, with rates 1 and 2.
The area rate is L′W+LW′=1(5)+5(2)=15.

items.prompt: A total cost is C(q)=q p(q), where p(10)=8 dollars per unit and p′(10)=−0.2 dollars per unit squared. Find C′(10).
steps: Product differentiation gives p(q)+q p′(q).

items.prompt: For f(x)=(x^2−1)/(x−1), compare its derivative with that of x+1 and state the domain difference.
items.answer: Both derivative formulas are 1 where x≠1; the original f has no derivative at 1.
steps: Factoring and cancelling gives x+1 only on the original domain.
The missing function value at 1 prevents a derivative there even though the simplified extension is smooth.

items.prompt: Construct two nonconstant polynomial functions whose product has derivative zero at x=0.
steps: Their product is x^2−1.
Its derivative 2x vanishes at zero even though neither factor is constant.

items.prompt: A ratio R(t)=A(t)/B(t) has A=12, A′=3, B=4, B′=1 at a given time. Is R increasing at that instant?
steps: The quotient numerator is 3(4)−12(1)=0.
Divide by 16 to get zero; the numerator and denominator are growing at matching relative rates.

items.prompt: Differentiate f(x)=(x^2+1)^2 using a product of equal factors, without a composition rule.
steps: Product rule gives 2x(x^2+1)+(x^2+1)2x, which combines as stated.

weeks.title: The chain rule
weeks.objective: Differentiate nested powers and identify each factor’s role in a changing-input chain.

connection.before: Product rules connect multiplying functions; composition feeds one output into another.
connection.after: Mixed derivative tasks will require choosing the outside operation before applying rules.

days: Draw input-to-output chains.
Multiply outer and inner rates.
Differentiate roots and negative powers of expressions.
Use composite derivative data from tables.
Find tangent slopes while retaining domain restrictions.
explanation: If y=f(u) and u=g(x), the chain rule gives dy/dx=f′(g(x))g′(x). First differentiate the outer function while leaving its input as a placeholder; then evaluate that derivative at the actual inner expression and multiply by the inner derivative. The evaluation point matters: f′(g(x)) is usually not f′(x).

For [g(x)]^n, the rule becomes n[g(x)]^(n−1)g′(x). The derivative of the inner expression is essential, even if it is only a constant. When the inner expression is nonlinear, forgetting it changes the shape of the derivative rather than just a coefficient. A chain can have several layers; work from the outside inward and include each changing link once.

A composition has the domain inherited from all its stages. Differentiating a root or reciprocal may narrow where a finite derivative formula is usable. Tables also support the chain rule: to find (f∘g)′(a), obtain g(a), then look up f′ at that output, and finally multiply by g′(a). A units check provides another route: outer units per intermediate unit times intermediate units per input unit gives the required final rate.

examples.prompt: Differentiate y=(2x^2−3)^4.
steps: The outer fourth power has derivative 4u^3.
Evaluate at u=2x^2−3 and multiply by u′=4x.
Combining factors gives 16x(2x^2−3)^3.

examples.prompt: Find the tangent slope of y=√(5x+4) at x=1.
steps: The outer derivative of √u is 1/(2√u).
Multiplying by the inner derivative 5 gives y′=5/(2√(5x+4)).
At x=1 the root is 3, so the slope is 5/6.

worksheets.title: Name and differentiate each layer
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: Differentiate (3x+2)^5.
steps: Apply the power rule to the outer fifth power.
Multiply 5(3x+2)^4 by the inner derivative 3.

items.prompt: Differentiate (1−x^2)^3.
steps: The outer derivative supplies 3(1−x^2)^2.
The inner derivative is −2x, yielding the negative factor.

items.prompt: Find d/dx of 1/(x^2+4).
steps: Rewrite the reciprocal as (x^2+4)^(−1).
Differentiate the outer power and multiply by 2x.

items.prompt: For x>−1/2, differentiate √(2x+1).
steps: The root derivative supplies 1/[2√(2x+1)].
The inner derivative 2 cancels the coefficient 2 in the denominator.

items.prompt: Identify inner and outer functions for y=(x^3−2x)^7 and write its derivative without expansion.
steps: The outer operation is the seventh power.
Multiply its derivative at the inner expression by the inner derivative 3x^2−2.
The outer derivative must be evaluated at g(2)=5.
Multiply f′(5)=4 by g′(2)=−3.

worksheets.title: Connect nested structures
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: Differentiate [1+(2x−1)^2]^3.
steps: Differentiate the cube, leaving its whole input intact.
The inner square contributes 2(2x−1) times 2, giving the total factor 12(2x−1).

items.prompt: Find the derivative of (x^2−1)^(−2), where x≠±1.
steps: The outer exponent gives −2(x^2−1)^(−3).
Multiplication by the inner derivative 2x gives the numerator −4x.

items.prompt: For f(x)=(x−4)^6, find every horizontal-tangent input.
steps: Differentiate to get 6(x−4)^5.
Its only zero is 4, a legal polynomial input.

items.prompt: Find the tangent line to y=(x^2+2)^2 at x=1.
steps: The curve value is (1+2)^2=9.
The chain derivative 4x(x^2+2) gives slope 12 at 1.

items.prompt: A learner gives d/dx of (4−3x)^2 as 2(4−3x). Correct it and explain the missing factor.
steps: The displayed result differentiates only the outer square.
The inner expression changes at rate −3, which must multiply the outer rate.

items.prompt: If f′(u)=2u and g(x)=x^2+1, find (f∘g)′(3) without finding f.
steps: At x=3, g=10 and g′=6.
The outer derivative is f′(10)=20, so the composite rate is 20(6).

worksheets.title: Interpret chained rates
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: A sphere’s volume is V(r)=(4/3)πr^3 and its radius is r(t)=1+2t cm, with t in seconds. Find dV/dt at t=1.
steps: At t=1 the radius is 3 and dr/dt=2.
The chain rule gives 4πr^2 dr/dt=4π(9)(2).

items.prompt: A cost C(A)=3A^2 dollars depends on area A(s)=s^2 square meters. Find dC/ds at s=2 m.
steps: The composite is 3s^4, whose derivative is 12s^3.
Evaluating at 2 gives 96, agreeing with (6A)(2s) at A=4.

items.prompt: For f(x)=√(9−x^2), state the derivative and where it is finite.
steps: The chain rule contributes inner derivative −2x and the outer factor 1/(2√(9−x^2)).
The original endpoints are allowed for f but make the derivative denominator zero.

items.prompt: Could (f∘g)′(a) be zero when f′(g(a)) is nonzero? State the needed condition and give an example.
items.answer: Yes, if g′(a)=0; for example f(u)=2u and g(x)=x^2 at a=0.
steps: The chain derivative is a product.
In the example its factors are 2 and 0, so the composite derivative is zero.

items.prompt: Let f(x)=(x^2−4)^2. Find the tangent slope at x=0 and explain why the inner derivative matters.
steps: The outer derivative at inner value −4 is −8.
Multiplying by the inner derivative 2x=0 gives zero; omitting it would falsely give −8.

items.prompt: A length ℓ(t) changes at 0.4 m/s and A(ℓ) has derivative 7 m^2 per meter at the current length. Find dA/dt.
steps: Multiply the area-per-length rate by the length-per-time rate.
The intermediate meter units cancel and 7(0.4)=2.8.

weeks.title: Choosing rules in a complete derivative
weeks.objective: Differentiate mixed rational and composite expressions and explain structural decisions.

connection.before: Product, quotient, and chain rules address distinct outside operations.
connection.after: New trig, exponential, and logarithmic rules will join this same structural framework.

days: Identify the last operation in each expression.
Combine product and chain rules.
Simplify a quotient derivative without losing restrictions.
Use tables at transformed inputs.
Critique a full solution and verify a derivative numerically.
explanation: Before differentiating, identify the expression’s outermost operation. A sum allows termwise work; a product requires two contributions; a quotient requires a squared denominator; and a composition multiplies rates through its layers. The same function can sometimes be written in several ways. Choose the representation that keeps the calculation short while making domain restrictions visible.

In a mixed expression, organize the work into named factors or inner functions. For u(x)[v(x)]^n, the product derivative includes u′[v]^n plus u·n[v]^(n−1)v′. The inner derivative belongs only to the factor being differentiated at that step. Keeping the expression factored often exposes zeros and signs more clearly than a long expansion.

A derivative can be checked by a second algebraic method or by small symmetric secant slopes at ordinary domain points. Numerical agreement is evidence, not a proof of a formula for every input, and it can fail near corners or singularities. Tables support exact derivative computations only when they supply every value required at the correct transformed inputs. Do not replace an unavailable entry by a nearby one.

examples.prompt: Differentiate f(x)=x(1+x^2)^3 and factor the result.
steps: Product rule gives (1+x^2)^3+x·3(1+x^2)^2·2x.
Factor out the common nonzero polynomial factor (1+x^2)^2.
The remaining sum is 1+x^2+6x^2=1+7x^2.

examples.prompt: Differentiate g(x)=[x/(x+1)]^2 for x≠−1.
steps: The outer square contributes 2[x/(x+1)].
The inner quotient derivative is [(x+1)−x]/(x+1)^2=1/(x+1)^2.
Multiply and simplify, retaining the original exclusion −1.

worksheets.title: Select the outside operation
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: Differentiate x^2(x+1)^4 and leave the answer factored.
steps: Product rule gives 2x(x+1)^4+4x^2(x+1)^3.
Factor 2x(x+1)^3 to combine (x+1)+2x.

items.prompt: Differentiate (2x+1)/(x^2+1).
steps: Quotient numerator is 2(x^2+1)−(2x+1)2x.
Expanding it gives −2x^2−2x+2.

items.prompt: Differentiate √(x^2+5) for real x.
steps: The outer root derivative is 1/[2√(x^2+5)].
Multiply by 2x; the denominator is always positive.
Differentiate each summand using its own chain.
The respective inner derivatives are 2x and 3.

items.prompt: At a, u=2, u′=−1, v=3, v′=4. Find the derivative of u v^2 at a.
steps: Product and chain rules give u′v^2+2uvv′.
Substitution gives −9+2(2)(3)(4)=39.

items.prompt: For h(x)=f(2x+1), which f′ table entry is needed to find h′(3), and what multiplier is required?
steps: At x=3 the inner input is 7.
The inner rate is 2, so h′(3)=2f′(7).

worksheets.title: Coordinate several derivative rules
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: Differentiate (x^2−1)^2/(x+1) by simplifying first, keeping the original domain.
steps: The original equals (x−1)^2(x+1) for x≠−1.
Product differentiation gives 2(x−1)(x+1)+(x−1)^2, which factors as stated.

items.prompt: Find the tangent line to f(x)=x√(x+3) at x=1.
steps: The curve value is 2.
Product rule gives √(x+3)+x/[2√(x+3)], whose value at 1 is 2+1/4.

items.prompt: If f(2)=5, f′(2)=3, g(1)=2, and g′(1)=−4, find the derivative of [f(g(x))]^2 at x=1.
steps: The outer square contributes 2f(g(1))=10.
The remaining chain contributes f′(2)g′(1)=3(−4), giving −120.

items.prompt: Find all zeros of the derivative of f(x)=x/(x^2+4).
steps: The derivative is (4−x^2)/(x^2+4)^2.
Its denominator never vanishes, so solve only 4−x^2=0.

items.prompt: A learner differentiates x(x−1)^2 as (x−1)^2+2(x−1). Identify and correct the omission.
steps: In the second product-rule term, the first factor x must remain unchanged.
The learner omitted that unchanged factor while differentiating the second factor.

items.prompt: For f(x)=(x^2+1)/(x^2−1), find f′(x) and its domain.
steps: Quotient numerator is 2x(x^2−1)−2x(x^2+1)=−4x.
Retain the original denominator’s two exclusions.

worksheets.title: Verify and interpret a full derivative
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: For f(x)=x^4 at x=2, compute the symmetric secant [f(2.01)−f(1.99)]/0.02 and compare it with f′(2).
steps: Expanding the symmetric difference cancels even increment powers and gives 4(2)^3+4(2)(0.01)^2.
The small excess 0.0008 tends to zero with the increment, supporting the derivative value.
items.skill: Verify and interpret a full derivative

items.prompt: A rectangle has sides x and √(16−x^2), with 0<x<4. Differentiate its area with respect to x.
steps: Product rule gives √(16−x^2)−x^2/√(16−x^2).
Combine over the common denominator; the stated interval makes the dimensions positive.
items.skill: Verify and interpret a full derivative

items.prompt: Find a for which f(x)=(ax+1)^2 has f′(0)=6.
steps: The derivative is 2a(ax+1).
At zero it becomes 2a, so the condition requires a=3.
items.skill: Verify and interpret a full derivative

items.prompt: Does a numerical check of a proposed derivative at x=1 prove the formula everywhere? Give two distinct candidate functions that agree at 1.
items.answer: No; candidates d1(x)=2x and d2(x)=x+1 both equal 2 at 1 but differ elsewhere.
steps: A single value constrains only one input.
At x=0 the candidates give 0 and 1, demonstrating that agreement at 1 is insufficient.
items.skill: Verify and interpret a full derivative

items.prompt: Let f(x)=1/(1+x^2)^2. Find the sign of f′(x) for x>0.
steps: Chain differentiation gives −4x/(1+x^2)^3.
Its denominator is positive and its numerator is negative when x>0.
items.skill: Verify and interpret a full derivative

items.prompt: A device maps x to u=2x−1, then to v=u^2+3, then to y=1/v. Find dy/dx at x=1.
steps: At x=1, u=1 and v=4; the three local rates are 2, 2u=2, and −1/v^2=−1/16.
Multiply the rates to obtain 2·2·(−1/16)=−1/4.
items.skill: Verify and interpret a full derivative

weeks.title: Trigonometric and exponential rates
weeks.objective: Differentiate sine, cosine, tangent, and exponential functions using radians and composition rules.

connection.before: Identify products and compositions before choosing derivative rules.
connection.after: Logarithmic and inverse-trigonometric derivatives will reverse several of these relationships.

days: Connect radian sine limits to trig derivatives.
Differentiate periodic models with frequency factors.
Use the exponential rate rule.
Combine products with trig or exponential factors.
Interpret signs and units in oscillation and growth.
explanation: With angles measured in radians, d/dx(sin x)=cos x and d/dx(cos x)=−sin x. The minus sign reflects the decreasing cosine height just after zero. The tangent derivative is sec^2 x=1/cos^2 x where cosine is nonzero. Degree-based inputs require an additional π/180 factor; the standard formulas in this course always use radians.

The natural exponential e^x has derivative e^x. A composition e^(g(x)) therefore has derivative e^(g(x))g′(x). More generally, a^x for a>0 has derivative a^x ln a. An exponential remains positive while the sign of its inner rate decides whether the composite increases or decreases. The derivative has the same exponential factor, but its coefficient and units may change.

Oscillation models often use A sin(ωt+φ)+D. The vertical offset D does not affect the rate. Amplitude A scales it, and angular frequency ω contributes another multiplier through the chain rule. A zero position is not automatically a zero velocity: sine is changing fastest at some of its zero crossings, while its rate vanishes at its extreme heights.

examples.prompt: For y=4 sin(3x−π/2), find y′ and y′(0).
steps: Differentiate the outside sine to cosine.
Multiply by both the amplitude 4 and the inner derivative 3.
At zero the angle is −π/2, whose cosine is zero.

examples.prompt: Differentiate f(x)=x e^(2x).
steps: Product rule gives 1·e^(2x)+x·d/dx(e^(2x)).
The exponential chain derivative is 2e^(2x).
Factor the common exponential to obtain the answer.

Combining the products yields the difference of squares.

Factoring and cancellation within the numerator leaves xe^x.

At 1 the exponential is e^0=1.

items.prompt: Correct d/dx cos(5x)=5 sin(5x).

Differentiating cosine introduces a minus sign that the proposed answer omitted.

items.answer: 6 m/s; the offset changes height but not velocity.
steps: Differentiation gives h′(t)=6 cos(2t).
At zero cosine is 1, while the constant’s derivative is zero.

items.prompt: A model P(t)=50e^(0.04t) uses t in years. Express P′ as a multiple of P and find P′(0).
steps: Differentiation preserves the exponential and adds 0.04.
At t=0 the model value is 50, so its rate is 0.04(50).

items.prompt: For f(x)=sin x on [0,2π], list all horizontal-tangent inputs.
steps: The derivative is cos x.
Cosine is zero at exactly those two inputs in the interval.

items.prompt: Let f(x)=e^x sin x. Find its tangent at x=0.
steps: The curve value is e^0 sin 0=0.
Product differentiation gives e^x(sin x+cos x), which has value 1 at zero.

items.prompt: A formula uses an angle d in degrees: F(d)=sin(πd/180). Find F′(0) per degree.
steps: Applying the chain rule gives (π/180)cos(πd/180).
At zero cosine is 1, so the degree conversion factor remains.

items.prompt: For y=e^(−x) cos x, determine y′(0) and whether y is increasing or decreasing there.
steps: Product differentiation gives −e^(−x)(cos x+sin x).
At zero this equals −1, so nearby output change has negative slope.

weeks.title: Logarithms and inverse-function rates
weeks.objective: Differentiate logarithms and basic inverse trig functions with their domains and inverse meanings.

connection.before: Exponential and trigonometric derivatives describe forward function rates.
connection.after: Implicit differentiation will find rates when no explicit inverse formula is convenient.

days: Use the logarithm derivative on a positive domain.
Differentiate logarithmic compositions.
Apply inverse sine and arctangent rules.
Reverse a nonzero local slope.
Check inverse-function domains and distinguish reciprocal notation.
explanation: For x>0, d/dx(ln x)=1/x. More generally, ln(abs(g(x))) has derivative g′(x)/g(x) on intervals where g is nonzero; ln(g(x)) itself additionally requires g>0. A logarithm of a product can sometimes simplify differentiation, but log identities must respect their domains. Writing ln(x^2)=2 ln x would wrongly discard negative inputs unless x>0 is specified.

The inverse sine arcsin x returns an angle in [−π/2,π/2] and has derivative 1/√(1−x^2) for −1<x<1. Its endpoints are in the function domain but not in the finite derivative formula. The arctangent arctan x returns an angle in (−π/2,π/2) and has derivative 1/(1+x^2) for every real x. These inverse functions are different from the reciprocals of sine and tangent.

If a differentiable one-to-one function f has nonzero derivative at a, the inverse derivative at b=f(a) is 1/f′(a), subject to the local differentiability conditions. Input and output exchange roles, so the slopes are reciprocals at corresponding points, not at the same numerical input by default. This relationship can supply an inverse rate from a table without solving an inverse formula.

examples.prompt: Differentiate f(x)=ln(x^2+3).
steps: The logarithm’s argument is positive for every real x.
The outer logarithm derivative is reciprocal of that argument.
Multiply by the inner derivative 2x.

examples.prompt: A differentiable one-to-one f satisfies f(2)=7 and f′(2)=−4. Find (f^−1)′(7), assuming the inverse is differentiable there.
steps: The inverse maps input 7 back to 2.
Its slope is the reciprocal of the forward slope at that corresponding point.

items.prompt: Differentiate arctan x.

The inverse derivative rule simplifies to the displayed positive expression for all real x.

Multiply by 2 and require a positive derivative denominator.

items.prompt: Differentiate x ln x for x>0.
steps: Product rule gives ln x+x(1/x).
The second term simplifies to 1 on the given domain.

items.prompt: Differentiate ln(x^2) for x≠0 without restricting to positive x.
steps: Direct chain differentiation gives 2x/x^2.
Simplify on nonzero inputs; equivalently ln(x^2)=2 ln(abs(x)).

items.prompt: Find d/dx of arctan(3x^2).
steps: The outer derivative is 1/[1+(3x^2)^2].
Multiply by the inner derivative 6x.

items.prompt: Find the tangent slope to y=arcsin x at x=1/2.
steps: Substitute into 1/√(1−x^2).
The denominator is √(3/4)=√3/2.

items.prompt: For f(x)=x^3+x, find the inverse derivative at output 2.
steps: Solve f(a)=2: a=1; f is strictly increasing because 3x^2+1>0.
The forward slope at 1 is 4, so the inverse slope at 2 is 1/4.

items.prompt: A student writes d/dx ln(x+2)=1/x. Correct the formula and explain.
steps: The outer reciprocal is evaluated at the entire argument x+2.
Multiplying by its derivative 1 does not change that shifted denominator.

worksheets.title: Interpret inverse and logarithmic rates
worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.prompt: A response model R(t)=ln(1+t^2) uses t in seconds. Find R′(2) and its units if R is dimensionless.
steps: Chain differentiation gives 2t/(1+t^2).
At t=2 this is 4/5, with output units divided by seconds.

items.prompt: A one-to-one calibration C(T) has C(20)=8 and C′(20)=0.4 signal units per degree. Find the inverse rate at signal 8.
steps: The inverse derivative is the reciprocal 1/0.4.
Reversing input and output also reverses the rate units.

items.prompt: For f(x)=arctan x, compare f′(0) and f′(2), and explain what happens to slope far from zero.
items.answer: 1 and 1/5; the positive slope tends to zero as abs(x) grows.
steps: Evaluate 1/(1+x^2) at the two inputs.
Its denominator grows without bound at either end, making the reciprocal small.

items.prompt: Find all real x where the derivative of ln(x^2+1) equals zero.
steps: The derivative is 2x/(x^2+1).
The denominator is always positive, so only the numerator can vanish.

items.prompt: Why does the reciprocal-slope formula not give a finite inverse derivative for f(x)=x^3 at output zero?
items.answer: f′(0)=0, so the required nonzero-slope hypothesis fails; the cube-root inverse has a vertical tangent.
steps: The rule would require division by zero.
The inverse difference quotient is 1/h^(2/3), which grows without bound near zero.

items.prompt: Differentiate ln((x+1)^2+1) and determine its derivative’s sign for x<−1.
steps: The chain derivative divides the inner rate 2(x+1) by the positive argument.
The numerator is negative on that interval, establishing the sign.

weeks.title: Implicit curves and their tangent directions
weeks.objective: Differentiate relations containing x and y while respecting local branches and denominator restrictions.

connection.before: The chain rule differentiates a dependent quantity, and inverse rules connect corresponding slopes.
connection.after: Derivative signs and critical numbers will organize a function’s global behavior.

days: Differentiate y as a function of x.
Collect terms containing y′.
Find tangent lines at supplied curve points.
Distinguish horizontal from vertical tangent candidates.
Check both the relation and the derivative denominator.
explanation: An equation such as x^2+y^2=R^2 describes a relation that may contain several y values for one x. Near a point where a smooth branch can be written as y(x), differentiate both sides with respect to x. Because y depends on x, the derivative of y^2 is 2y y′. Treating y as constant would remove the very rate being sought.

After differentiation, collect every y′ term on one side and factor it out before dividing. Products such as xy require x y′+y, while a composite function of y requires its own chain factor y′. Substitute a point only after the differentiation is correct, and first confirm that the point lies on the original relation. A formally computed slope at an off-curve point is not a tangent slope to that curve.

If a solved formula for y′ has a zero denominator, it does not give a finite slope there. A vertical tangent may occur, but numerator and denominator structure need inspection. A horizontal tangent instead requires numerator zero with denominator nonzero. Implicit differentiation is local; it does not turn a multi-branch relation into one globally defined function.

examples.prompt: For x^2+y^2=25, find the tangent line at (3,4).
steps: The point satisfies 9+16=25.
Differentiating gives 2x+2y y′=0, hence y′=−x/y for y≠0.
At (3,4) the slope is −3/4, giving the point-slope equation.

examples.prompt: Find y′ for xy+y^2=6, and evaluate it at (1,2).
steps: Product and chain rules give y+x y′+2y y′=0.
Collect y′ to obtain (x+2y)y′=−y.
The point satisfies 2+4=6 and its denominator is 5, giving −2/5.

At the point, 4+2y′=0, so y′=−2.

items.prompt: Find y′ from y^3+x=9.

Divide by the nonzero coefficient of y′ to isolate the rate.

items.prompt: For x^2+y^2=16, identify the horizontal-tangent points.

Substituting x=0 in the relation gives y=±4.

items.answer: The factor y′; the derivative is 4y^3 y′.
steps: The fourth power is an outer function of y.
The chain rule multiplies its derivative by the inner rate dy/dx.

items.prompt: Does (2,3) lie on x^2+y^2=10? May the circle’s tangent there be requested?
items.answer: No; 4+9=13≠10, so it is not a curve point.
steps: Substitute both coordinates into the defining equation.

worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

steps: Differentiate to 3x^2+3y^2y′=6y+6xy′.
Collect and divide: (3y^2−6x)y′=6y−3x^2.

steps: Differentiation gives 2x+y+(x+2y)y′=0.
At the point the numerator is −(2+2)=−4 and denominator is 5.

steps: Differentiate to e^y y′+1=0.
Divide by the positive e^y, then substitute y=0.

items.prompt: For sin y=x near (0,0), find y′ and compare with the inverse-sine derivative there.
steps: Differentiation gives cos y·y′=1.
At y=0 the cosine is 1; the inverse-sine formula also gives 1/√1.

items.prompt: Find the tangent line to x^2+4y^2=20 at (2,2).
steps: The point satisfies 4+16=20.
The derivative −x/(4y) gives −2/8=−1/4 there.

items.prompt: For x^2+y^2=9, explain the tangent direction at (3,0).
items.answer: Vertical; the tangent line is x=3.
steps: In the local expression x=√(9−y^2), dx/dy=−y/x is zero at that point.
Thus the curve has horizontal change zero per vertical change, while y′=−x/y is not finite.

items.prompt: A curve is x^2+y^2=2x. Find its horizontal-tangent points.
steps: Differentiation gives y′=(1−x)/y, so a zero slope needs x=1 and y≠0.
Substituting x=1 gives 1+y^2=2, hence y=±1.

steps: Factoring y gives (x+1)y=3.
Explicit differentiation agrees with implicit y′=−y/(x+1) after substituting the solved y.

items.answer: The two branches have opposite nonzero y values, so −x/y has opposite signs when x≠0.
steps: The circle does not globally define one y for each x.
At x=0 both slopes are zero; elsewhere the two local branches have different tangent directions.

items.prompt: Find the tangent slope at (0,1) on y^2+x y=1.
steps: Differentiating gives 2y y′+y+x y′=0.

items.prompt: For x=y^2, locate the point where y′ is not finite and state the tangent line.
steps: Differentiation gives 1=2y y′, so division fails at y=0.
The parameterization x=y^2 has dx/dy=0 there, confirming the vertical direction.

items.prompt: For ln y+x^2=0 with y>0, find y′ at x=1.
steps: The relation gives y=e^(−x^2), so at 1, y=e^(−1).
Implicit differentiation gives y′/y+2x=0, hence y′=−2xy.

weeks.title: Critical numbers and extreme values
weeks.objective: Find and compare candidate extrema while separating local behavior from absolute bounds.

connection.before: Derivative formulas identify inputs with zero or undefined slope.
connection.after: The Mean Value Theorem and sign tests will explain how derivatives control whole intervals.

days: Name local and absolute extrema precisely.
Locate critical numbers inside the domain.
Apply the closed-interval candidate method.
Include endpoints and nondifferentiable candidates.
Check the Extreme Value Theorem hypotheses and counterexamples.
explanation: A local maximum is at least as high as nearby values; an absolute maximum is at least as high as every value in the specified domain. The domain matters: changing a closed interval to an open one can remove an attained extreme value. A critical number is an interior input in the function’s domain where the derivative is zero or fails to exist. A denominator exclusion is not a critical number because the function is absent there.

The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that a function continuous on a closed, bounded interval attains an absolute maximum and minimum. For a differentiable interior extremum, Fermat’s theorem gives f′=0. Together these facts motivate the closed-interval method: list interior critical numbers and the two endpoints, evaluate the original function at each, then compare the values. The derivative values are not the heights being optimized.

A critical number is only a candidate. The function x^3 has zero derivative at zero but no local extremum there. Corners can be extrema even without a derivative, and endpoints may be absolute extrema without zero slope. If continuity or compactness fails, the theorem no longer guarantees attainment; analyze the actual function instead of claiming extrema cannot exist.

examples.prompt: Find absolute extrema of f(x)=x^3−3x on [−2,3].
examples.answer: Absolute minimum −2 at x=−2 and x=1; absolute maximum 18 at x=3.
steps: Critical numbers solve 3x^2−3=0, giving −1 and 1 inside the interval.
Evaluate f at −2,−1,1,3 to get −2,2,−2,18.
The polynomial is continuous on the closed interval, so comparing this complete candidate list finds the absolute extrema.

examples.prompt: Find absolute extrema of g(x)=abs(x−1) on [−1,4].
examples.answer: Minimum 0 at x=1; maximum 3 at x=4.
steps: The corner at 1 is an interior critical number even though no derivative exists there.
Candidate values at −1,1,4 are 2,0,3.
Continuity and the closed interval justify comparing endpoints and the corner.

Its zeros are ±2, and the polynomial has no undefined derivative inputs.

A critical number must be an input where the function itself exists.

items.answer: Minimum 0 at x=0; maximum 9 at x=3.
steps: The interior critical number is 0.
Compare f(−1)=1, f(0)=0, and f(3)=9.

items.prompt: Does f(x)=x have a maximum on (0,1)?
steps: Every allowed x can be replaced by the larger allowed input (x+1)/2.
Values approach 1 but never attain it, because the endpoint is excluded.

items.prompt: Is x=0 a local extremum of f(x)=x^3?
steps: Nearby negative inputs give negative values and positive inputs give positive values.
The function passes through zero despite its zero derivative there.

items.prompt: Which theorem guarantees extrema for a continuous function on [2,8]? State its hypotheses.
items.answer: The Extreme Value Theorem: continuity on a closed, bounded interval.
steps: The interval includes its endpoints and has finite length.
These properties plus continuity guarantee attained absolute maximum and minimum.

worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning that supports each answer. Use exact values unless rounding is requested. All angles are in radians. For a justification or construction, equivalent valid responses are acceptable.

items.answer: Minimum −3 at x=2; maximum 6 at x=5.
steps: The critical input from 2x−4=0 is 2.
Candidate values are 1,−3,6 at 0,2,5.

items.answer: Minimum 0 at x=0; maximum 4 at x=−8.
steps: Zero is an interior critical input where the derivative is undefined.
The candidate values at −8,0,1 are 4,0,1.

steps: Derivative zeros inside the interval include π/2.
Compare its height with endpoint values 0 and −1; the final endpoint also has zero slope.

items.answer: Minimum 2 at x=1; maximum 10/3 at x=3.
steps: The derivative 1−1/x^2 vanishes at the only positive interior candidate 1.
The values at 1/2,1,3 are 5/2,2,10/3.

items.answer: Minimum 1 at x=1; maximum 4 at x=2.
steps: There are no interior critical numbers, but endpoints remain candidates.
The continuous function increases across the closed interval and attains both endpoint extrema.

items.prompt: For f(x)=−abs(x+2), identify and classify its interior critical number on [−5,1].
items.answer: x=−2; it is an absolute and local maximum with value 0.
steps: The corner has no derivative but lies in the domain.
Every other input gives the negative of a positive magnitude, so its value is lower.
